overview.title: Symbolic tensors and the Model constructor
overview.section: 7.2 Different ways to build Keras models
overview.main_topic: Step-by-step explanation of Listing 7.8: what a symbolic tensor is, how layers called on symbolic tensors return new symbolic tensors, and how keras.Model is built from inputs and outputs.
overview.central_idea: keras.Input returns a symbolic tensor — a data-free placeholder carrying shape and dtype that stands for future tensors. Calling layers on symbolic tensors produces new symbolic tensors with updated shapes, and keras.Model(inputs, outputs) captures the resulting graph of layers.
overview.importance: The symbolic tensor is the core mechanism of the Functional API. Understanding it explains why Functional models are built immediately, why Keras can inspect their structure, and how multi-input/multi-output models (next page) are wired.
learning_objectives: Define a symbolic tensor and explain what it does and does not contain.
Explain that layers accept both real and symbolic tensors, returning a symbolic tensor in the latter case.
Describe how keras.Model is instantiated from inputs and outputs.
Read a Functional model summary, including the InputLayer row with 0 parameters.
prerequisites: keras.Input and the None batch dimension (pp.217-218)

summary:
This page walks through Listing 7.8 line by line.

**The input.** `inputs = keras.Input(shape=(3,), name="my_input")` produces an object that holds the **shape** and **dtype** of the data the model will process: `inputs.shape` is `(None, 3)` and `inputs.dtype` is `"float32"`. The callouts explain: the model will process batches where each sample has shape `(3,)`, the number of samples per batch is variable (the `None`), and the batches will have dtype float32.

The book calls this a **symbolic tensor**: it *doesn't contain any actual data*, but it *encodes the specifications* of the actual data tensors the model will see. It *stands for* future tensors of data.

**Calling a layer.** `features = layers.Dense(64, activation="relu")(inputs)` creates a layer and calls it on the input. **All Keras layers can be called on real tensors or on symbolic tensors**; on a symbolic tensor they return **a new symbolic tensor with updated shape and dtype**, so `features.shape` is `(None, 64)`.

**Building the model.** After getting the final `outputs = layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")(features)`, the model is created with `keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs, name="my_functional_model")`.

**The summary** of `"my_functional_model"` lists three rows: `my_input (InputLayer)` `(None, 3)` with **0** parameters, `dense_8 (Dense)` `(None, 64)` 256, and `dense_9 (Dense)` `(None, 10)` 650. Unlike the Sequential summaries on pp.217-219, the Functional summary shows the input as its own `InputLayer` row; the named input appears as `my_input`.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The inputs object records the shape and dtype of the data the model will process: (None, 3) and float32.
paragraphs.what_it_means: shape=(3,) in keras.Input becomes (None, 3): Keras prepends a batch axis of unknown size. dtype defaults to float32.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: These two pieces of information are all a downstream layer needs to create its weights, which is why Functional models are built as soon as they are defined.

The number of samples per batch is variable.

paragraphs.excerpt: We call such an object a symbolic tensor. It doesn’t contain any
paragraphs.what_it_says: Such an object is a symbolic tensor: it has no data but encodes the specifications of the actual tensors the model will see; it stands for future tensors of data.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A symbolic tensor is a placeholder in a graph-under-construction. Operations on it record structure (which layer consumes what) and propagate shape/dtype, without performing any arithmetic.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is what lets the Functional API describe a model's computation graph ahead of time and lets Keras inspect, summarize and plot it.
paragraphs.technical_idea: In Keras 3 these are KerasTensor objects; they also remember which layer call produced them, which is how keras.Model can trace back from outputs to inputs.

terminology.meaning: A data-free object specifying the shape and dtype of tensors that will flow through a model; stands for future data.

connections: p.219: Listing 7.8 creates the symbolic input.

paragraphs.excerpt: Next, we created a layer and called it on the input:
paragraphs.what_it_says: The second step creates a Dense layer and calls it on the input.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Dense(64, activation="relu") constructs the layer; the trailing (inputs) calls it. Because the input shape (3) is known, the layer is built (kernel (3, 64)) at this moment.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Creating and calling in one expression is the idiomatic Functional style.
connections: p.217: layers get built when they are called for the first time.

paragraphs.excerpt: All Keras layers can be called both on real tensors of data
paragraphs.what_it_says: Layers can be called on real tensors or symbolic tensors; on symbolic tensors they return a new symbolic tensor with updated shape and dtype.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The same layer object serves both to define a graph (symbolic call) and to compute (eager call on arrays). The output symbolic tensor's shape is the layer's computed output shape, here (None, 64).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This duality is why a Functional model is just a reusable function: after construction, calling model(real_data) runs the same layers on real tensors.

terminology.meaning: A tensor holding actual numerical data (e.g. a NumPy array or backend tensor).

connections: p.221: multi-input models use the same mechanism with several Input objects.

paragraphs.what_it_says: With the final outputs in hand, the model is created by passing inputs and outputs to the Model constructor.
paragraphs.what_it_means: keras.Model walks the graph from outputs back to inputs, collecting every layer call in between. Anything not on a path between them is excluded.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The model is defined entirely by its endpoints, which is what makes multi-input and multi-output models straightforward: pass lists (or dicts) of tensors.

terminology.meaning: keras.Model(inputs=..., outputs=..., name=...) builds a model from symbolic tensors.

concepts.name: Symbolic tensor
concepts.definition: An object that contains no data but encodes the shape and dtype of the tensors a model will process; it stands for future tensors of data.
concepts.intuition: A blueprint label on an empty conveyor belt: 'batches of 3 float32 numbers will travel here'.
concepts.technical: Returned by keras.Input; calling a layer on it returns another symbolic tensor with the layer's output shape/dtype, and records the connection.
concepts.significance: The mechanism underpinning the Functional API.
concepts.misconception: That inputs holds a batch of data or random values; it holds none.

concepts.name: Functional API
concepts.definition: Building models by calling layers on symbolic tensors and passing inputs/outputs to keras.Model.
concepts.intuition: Wire the graph, then box it up.
concepts.misconception: That the model must be compiled or called to be built; Functional models are built when constructed.

concepts.name: Keras layer (dual call)
concepts.definition: A Keras layer is callable on real tensors (computes) or symbolic tensors (records structure and returns a symbolic output).
concepts.intuition: The same machine can run on real parts or be drawn into a factory plan.
concepts.technical: On symbolic input the layer is built if needed and its output spec is computed.
concepts.significance: Lets one object serve for both model definition and computation.
concepts.misconception: That you need different layer classes for graph definition and execution.

model = keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs, name="my_functional_model")
code.what_it_does: Produces the output tensor and wraps the graph from inputs to outputs into a named Model.

deeper.title: Symbolic vs eager: two modes of the same layer
deeper.body:
AI explanation of what the page describes:
1. `keras.Input(shape=(3,))` → symbolic tensor `(None, 3)`, float32. No numbers exist.
2. `Dense(64)(inputs)`: the layer sees a symbolic tensor, builds its `(3, 64)` kernel and `(64,)` bias, computes the output spec `(None, 64)`, and records "this tensor came from this layer applied to that tensor".
3. `Dense(10)(features)`: same, giving `(None, 10)`.
4. `keras.Model(inputs, outputs)` follows those records backward to collect the layers.
5. Later, `model(x)` with a real array replays the recorded layer calls in eager mode, now doing arithmetic.

deeper.title: Symbolic tensors as function parameters
deeper.body: When you write `def f(x): return 2 * x + 1`, `x` is not a number — it stands for any future number. A symbolic tensor plays the same role for a model: `inputs` is the parameter name, the layer calls are the function body, and `keras.Model(inputs, outputs)` is the `def`.

misconceptions.claim: A symbolic tensor contains a dummy batch of data.
misconceptions.correction: It contains no data at all; it only encodes shape and dtype specifications.

misconceptions.claim: Layers need special versions to be called on symbolic tensors.
misconceptions.correction: All Keras layers can be called on both real and symbolic tensors.

misconceptions.claim: The InputLayer in the summary adds parameters.
misconceptions.correction: It has 0 parameters; it only represents the input in the graph.

earlier.note: Layers are built when first called; None batch dimension.

later.note: The Functional API gives direct access to layer connectivity.

takeaways: keras.Input returns a symbolic tensor with shape (None, 3) and dtype float32.
A symbolic tensor holds no data; it stands for future tensors.
Layers called on symbolic tensors return new symbolic tensors with updated shape/dtype.
keras.Model(inputs=..., outputs=...) defines the model by its endpoints.
The Functional summary includes an InputLayer row with 0 parameters.

questions.question: What does the inputs object returned by keras.Input(shape=(3,)) contain?
options: A batch of zeros of shape (1, 3)
The shape and dtype specification of future data, but no data
The weights of the first layer
questions.answer: The shape and dtype specification of future data, but no data
questions.explanation: The page defines it as a symbolic tensor that doesn't contain actual data. It is not a zero batch or array, and weights belong to layers.

questions.question: What is features.shape after features = layers.Dense(64, activation="relu")(inputs)?
questions.explanation: The layer returns a new symbolic tensor with updated shape: last axis 64, batch axis unchanged.

questions.question: What does the None in inputs.shape signify?
questions.answer: The number of samples per batch is variable.
questions.explanation: From the callout next to inputs.shape.

questions.question: Why does the Functional summary list my_input (InputLayer) with 0 parameters when the Sequential summaries did not list the input?
questions.answer: In the Functional model the input is an explicit node of the layer graph (an InputLayer), so it appears in the summary; it has no weights, hence 0 parameters.
questions.explanation: Compare p.220's table with p.219's. The 'why' is an AI explanation of what the tables show.

questions.question: Using the three rows of the summary, what is the total parameter count of my_functional_model?
Which statement about calling Keras layers is correct according to the page?
options: Layers can only be called on symbolic tensors inside a Functional model
Layers can be called on real tensors or symbolic tensors
Layers called on symbolic tensors return real tensors
Layers called on symbolic tensors return None
questions.answer: Layers can be called on real tensors or symbolic tensors
questions.explanation: The page says all Keras layers can be called on both; on symbolic tensors they return a new symbolic tensor, not a real one or None.

questions.question: Can you explain to someone, without code, why a Functional model can be summarized immediately after construction while the Sequential model of Listing 7.2 could not?
questions.answer: The Functional model starts from an Input with known shape, so every layer is built during the symbolic calls; Listing 7.2 had no input shape, so its layers had no weights yet.
